messages.subject: Filters for noise reduction
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I already posted a message on this forum in November but unfortunately I did not get an answer, so I come back !

I remind you that we made an experiment in natural environment to study sound detection, localization and propagation.

We installed a microphones array of 20 automatic recording units and we played a synthetic sound (mixed pure tones, with fundamental frequencies ranging from 300 to 1000 Hz).

We are looking for a noise reduction algorithm (for example median noise filter) and then applying an automatic detector.

After much research, I unfortunately don’t found automated methods to reduce background noise without damaging my signal. I found some Matlab scripts and I would like to know if similar scripts or functions exist with Seewave or R.

Once again, I would be very grateful if you have any advice for me.

Best regards,

Morgane PAPIN

messages.subject: Re: Filters for noise reduction
messages.body_plain:
Dear Morgane,
We also did sound propagation measurements. I could post the link here once the manuscript is accepted.

So we had to extract our emitted test sounds too. They were organized in groups of a specific structure (a step signal), so all we needed to do was to manually extract each group of signals and then use R to analyse the different test sounds at predetermined time and frequency coordinates. We did not use noise reduction, and I would not rely on that for extracting my test sounds except if I were 100% certain that it would not damage the test sounds I want to measure. I expect the faraway signals to be very hard to discern from background noise.

Apart from this, you will probably want to quantify the background sound level anyway.
Best,
Kevin Darras

messages.subject: ACI
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I have a question about the "ACI" function in seewave?

I am calculating ACI values for 5 minute chunks of my recordings.  Going through the ACI function it is unclear what is used as 'temporal steps' (Eq. 2 "j"; Pieretti et al. 2011).  I'm assuming it's the window size from the FFT?  Also, I'm wondering if there's a way to change the temporal step size?  For example, if I want to compare 1 minute steps?  The reason I ask is that I'd like to make the ACI values comparable to AR (where the user defines the size of the temporal step - which I've defined as 1 minute).

Thanks very much for your help,

Rachel

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] ACI
messages.body_plain:
Dear Rachel,

The 'temporal steps' is encoded in the argument 'nbwindows'. It does not match exactly the definition of the ACI but does exactly the same. The idea is that you do not provide a step in duration but that you give a number of steps.
For instance, if you have a 5' recording setting up 'nbwindows=5' will compute the ACI with temporal steps of 1'.
As far as I can remember, there is no predefined temporal step for AR. AR takes the complete file (recording) as an input.

HTH

Jerome

messages.subject: Question: meanspec() and spec() functions
messages.body_plain:
I'm new to seewave and would really appreciate some help on the following:

I'm currently extracting some frequency parameters from bat calls from ultrasonic recordings - using functions such as fpeaks(), specprop() and fbands(), which all require input of a frequency spectrum. There are two ways of doing this; meanspec() which is based on the mean relative amplitude of the frequency distribution, and spec() based on the relative amplitude of the frequency distribution. Because my results differ depending on which one of the two I use, can anybody explain to me what exactly the difference is? What is spec() relative to and how is it computed?

Cheers!

Kat

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Question: meanspec() and spec() functions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Katarina,

spec() is basically the modulus of the FFT of the signal you provide
as an input.
meanspec() is the average of a STFT applied to the signal provided, it
is therefore the average of successive FFTs, in other words the
average of the results of successive spec().
The AM and FM of the signal will be represented differently using
either spec() and meanspec() and the length (number of frequency
samples) may also differ greatly.
It is therefore not surprising that you got different results.

HTH a bit,

Jerome

messages.subject: Spec function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I’m doing this little exercise:

> a <- readWave(file=file.choose(),header=FALSE)

> enva = env(a, norm = FALSE, envt="abs")
> amp_value = mean(enva)

> speca = spec(a, norm = FALSE)
> amp_value = mean(speca[,2])

I was expecting to get similar absolute amplitude values from both methods.
As I understand it the mean of env(a) provides de average absolute amplitude of my recording. As spec(a) second column gives the amplitude per frequency band from my recording, should not the mean of this column give a similar result, i.e. the recording absolute amplitude average?

However, results differ in three orders of magnitude (716.7 vs. 187464.4)

Why amplitude values from spec are higher?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Spec function
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Using env() and meanspec() cannot give similar results in terms of energy. The equivalent of energy between the time and frequency domains is not direct. It is ruled out by the Parseval's theorem <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parseval%27s_theorem> that you can check with:

data(tico)
time <- sum(tico@left^2)
fspec <- Mod(fft(tico@left))
N <- length(fspec)
frequency <- 1/N*sum(fspec^2)
time - frequency

HTH

Jerome
